Measurement error in assay data: what the weights mean

An additive model, reliability, censoring, and a glossary for immunologists

Source: vignettes/measurement-error.Rmd
measurement-error.Rmd

Who this is for. You know linear models, random effects and likelihoods, and you know your assay. You have not necessarily met measurement-error models, the branch of statistics that separates “the sample really differs” from “the assay read it imprecisely”. This page explains the one idea you need, how curveRweights uses it, and which numbers it hands you. A companion page, vignette("downstream-analysis"), shows what to do with those numbers.

The one idea: every reading is signal plus noise

Take one serum sample measured on a bead assay. The number you report, the back-calculated log10 concentration yiy_i, is built from three things:

yi=μgroup⏟the effect you study+bi⏟real biological spread+ei⏟assay measurement error y_i \;=\; \underbrace{\mu_{\text{group}}}_{\text{the effect you study}} \;+\; \underbrace{b_i}_{\text{real biological spread}} \;+\; \underbrace{e_i}_{\text{assay measurement error}}

  • μgroup\mu_{\text{group}} is the group mean, for example a vaccine arm at one time point. Estimating differences in μ\mu is usually the scientific question.
  • bib_i is true biological variation between people (or between samples): some people simply respond more strongly. It has variance τ2\tau^2. More assay precision never removes it.
  • eie_i is measurement error. The calibration curve tells us how large it is for this sample: the standard error se of the back-calculated concentration, so Var(ei)=vi=κ2sei2β1\text{Var}(e_i) = v_i = \kappa^2\,se_i^{2\beta_1}. Near the top and bottom of the standard curve the curve is flat, a small change in the signal means a large change in concentration, and viv_i is large. In the middle viv_i is small.

Because bib_i and eie_i are independent, their variances add:

σi2=τ2+vi=τ2+κ2sei2β1. \sigma_i^2 \;=\; \tau^2 + v_i \;=\; \tau^2 + \kappa^2\, se_i^{2\beta_1}.

This is the additive model. It is the same structure as a random-effects meta-analysis, where each study has a within-study variance viv_i (known) and the studies differ by a between-study variance τ2\tau^2 (estimated).

Why we weight at all

A weighted analysis gives precisely measured samples more say. The efficient weight is the inverse of the total variance:

wi=1τ2+vi. w_i = \frac{1}{\tau^2 + v_i}.

Look at what this does at the extremes:

  • A hopelessly noisy sample (vi→∞v_i \to \infty) gets weight near 0. Good.
  • A perfectly measured sample (vi→0v_i \to 0) gets weight 1/τ21/\tau^2, not infinity. Good: a perfect measurement of one person still tells you only about that person, and people differ by τ2\tau^2.

So the largest weight ratio you can ever see is bounded: wmax/wmin≤(τ2+vmax)/τ2w_{max}/w_{min} \le (\tau^2 + v_{max})/\tau^2.

Additive versus multiplicative

Versions of curveRweights before 0.3.0 used a multiplicative model, σi=ϕseiβ1\sigma_i = \phi\, se_i^{\beta_1}, so σi2=ϕ2sei2β1\sigma_i^2 = \phi^2 se_i^{2\beta_1}. Here all the variance is attributed to the measurement. A sample with a very small sese then gets a very large weight, with no ceiling, even when real person-to-person variation (the τ2\tau^2 above) would limit what that sample can tell you. The additive model puts a floor under σi\sigma_i and therefore a ceiling on wiw_i.

The simulation below uses the same seise_i values for both. The true model is additive with τ=0.4\tau = 0.4; we ask each approach what weights it implies.

set.seed(42)
se  <- exp(rnorm(2000, log(0.15), 0.9))          # a realistic spread of SEs
tau <- 0.4

w_add  <- 1 / (tau^2 + se^2)                      # additive: ceiling 1/tau^2 = 6.25
w_mult <- 1 / (1.1^2 * se^2)                      # multiplicative, phi = 1.1

ratio <- function(w) max(w) / min(w)
c(additive = ratio(w_add), multiplicative = ratio(w_mult))
#>       additive multiplicative 
#>       90.15707   274173.78492
c(`additive ceiling 1/tau^2` = 1 / tau^2,
  `multiplicative max weight` = max(w_mult))
#>  additive ceiling 1/tau^2 multiplicative max weight 
#>                      6.25                  15878.96

With the SE spread used here the multiplicative weights span a ratio of hundreds of thousands, against about 90 for the additive model, and its largest weight (about 16,000) is thousands of times the additive ceiling of 6.25. In a real analysis such a sample effectively is the group mean. That is the practical reason the additive model is the one to prefer when you analyse differences between people or groups and when between-subject variation is not negligible.

Which model do I get? fit_precision_weights() still defaults to model = "multiplicative" so that existing pipelines and results are unchanged; ask for the new one with model = "additive". In I-SPI the choice is recorded with every weight set (column model).

Situation Prefer
Comparing groups or time points; people differ a lot additive
Assay noise dominates and people barely differ (τ≈0\tau \approx 0) either; they agree
You must reproduce an earlier analysis the model you used then

Reliability: how much of what you see is real

The additive model gives each sample a reliability

λi=τ2τ2+vi∈(0,1]. \lambda_i \;=\; \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + v_i} \;\in\; (0, 1].

It is the fraction of that sample’s variance that is genuine biological signal. If you know the intraclass correlation (ICC) from repeated-measures work or from the Cronbach’s α\alpha of a questionnaire, this is the same idea applied sample by sample: 0.9 means “mostly signal”, 0.3 means “mostly assay noise”.

d <- data.frame(se_meas = c(0.03, 0.10, 0.30, 1.00))
out <- compute_additive_weights(d, tau2 = 0.16, kappa = 1)
out[, c("se_meas", "v_meas", "w", "reliability", "w_norm")]
#>   se_meas v_meas        w reliability    w_norm
#> 1    0.03  9e-04 6.215040   0.9944065 1.4658579
#> 2    0.10  1e-02 5.882353   0.9411765 1.3873914
#> 3    0.30  9e-02 4.000000   0.6400000 0.9434261
#> 4    1.00  1e+00 0.862069   0.1379310 0.2033246

Reliability is the number to show to collaborators. A weight depends on an arbitrary scale; a reliability does not. It also explains regression dilution, below.

Weights fix efficiency, not bias in predictors

Weights improve the precision of an estimate when the noisy variable is the outcome. When the noisy variable is a predictor (for example antibody level used to predict infection, or one antigen’s response correlated with another’s), weights do not repair it. Noise in a predictor flattens the fitted slope toward zero by roughly the factor λ\lambda (regression dilution or attenuation). Two remedies are included:

# a correlation of 0.42 between two noisy assays with mean reliabilities 0.85, 0.70
attenuation_correct(0.42, rel_x = 0.85, rel_y = 0.70)
#> [1] 0.5444911

reliability_correct() replaces each measured value by its best prediction of the true value (shrinking it toward its cell mean by λi\lambda_i), which removes the first-order bias of a regression slope. See vignette("downstream-analysis") for a worked example.

Samples outside the standard curve: censoring

A sample whose signal falls below the lowest standard is not “a noisy concentration”. It is a sample we know only to be below some limit. Giving such a value an ordinary weight is wrong: its precision is poor because the concentration is extreme, so inverse-variance weights down-weight the very samples that say “low”, and group means drift towards the middle of the curve.

The additive model treats these samples as censored:

  • left-censored: the true value is below the lower limit;
  • right-censored: above the upper limit;
  • interval: between two limits.

Quantified samples contribute the usual Normal density. A censored sample contributes the probability of being beyond its limit, so it informs the group mean and τ\tau without being treated as a precise point. In the weight table these rows carry censor_type and bound, and their w_norm is NA on purpose: represent them by the bound, not by a weight.

set.seed(3)
n   <- 20000
mu  <- c(low = 0.6, high = 2.0)
g   <- rep(names(mu), each = n)
tru <- rnorm(2 * n, rep(mu, each = n), 0.4)
se_fun <- function(y) 0.05 + 0.35 * plogis((0.5 - y) / 0.15) +
                              0.35 * plogis((y - 3.0) / 0.15)
obs <- tru + rnorm(2 * n, 0, se_fun(tru))
w   <- 1 / (0.4^2 + se_fun(obs)^2)               # additive weights, own-SE
rbind(truth      = mu,
      unweighted = tapply(obs, g, mean)[names(mu)],
      weighted   = tapply(obs * w, g, sum)[names(mu)] / tapply(w, g, sum)[names(mu)])
#>                  low     high
#> truth      0.6000000 2.000000
#> unweighted 0.5964011 2.002382
#> weighted   0.6928282 1.995671

Even with the additive ceiling the weighted mean of the low group (about 0.69) sits well above the truth (0.60), while the unweighted mean (0.60) does not; the high group is barely affected because most of it lies where precision is good. That is the reason the package treats out-of-range samples by their limits instead of weights. prepare_censoring() builds the flags from curveRcore’s censor_type, censor_lower and censor_upper.

Repeated measures and dilutions

If the same patient contributes several samples, their bib_i are not independent. fit_additive_weight() accepts a patient column and adds a patient random intercept, the familiar (1 | patientid), so the repeated measures are not over-counted. Dilutions or replicates of the same sample are handled with sample_col.

Note on units: the weights are on the log10 concentration scale, the scale the model is fitted on. When censoring is used, the model puts the response on the final concentration scale (it adds log10(dilution)\log_{10}(\text{dilution})), the same scale as the censoring limits curveRcore reports.

What the stored columns mean

When I-SPI or the i-spi-compute worker saves weights, each sample row (table calib_weights) holds:

Column Meaning
model multiplicative or additive
se the calibration curve’s SE for that sample (measurement SD, log10)
sigma total SD σi\sigma_i
w raw inverse-variance weight 1/σi21/\sigma_i^2
w_norm w divided by its mean over quantified rows (mean 1). NA for censored rows in the additive model
v_meas measurement variance viv_i (additive only). Use this for metafor
tau2 between-sample variance τ2\tau^2 (additive only)
reliability, _lo, _hi λi\lambda_i and a 95% interval (additive only)
censor_type, bound none / left / interval / right, and the limit (log10)
weights_pkg_version the curveRweights version that produced the row

Per curve group (calib_weights_fit) you also get τ\tau, κ\kappa, the group mean reliability, n_censored, whether β1\beta_1 was fixed, and an identifiability note. Column definitions live in code too: curveRcore::weights_contract().

How good is τ\tau? Identifiability

τ\tau (signal) and κ\kappa (the scale of the measurement error) can be separated only because the seise_i differ from sample to sample: when sese is large, the total variance is mostly measurement; when small, mostly τ2\tau^2. If all seise_i are nearly equal, the data cannot tell the two apart. By default β1\beta_1 is fixed at 1 (the theoretical value from the delta method) and κ\kappa is estimated. The fit reports a message when κ\kappa is weakly identified; treat τ\tau and the reliabilities from such a group as provisional, or fix κ=1\kappa = 1 and assume se is the true measurement SD.

Glossary

Term Plain meaning
Measurement error Difference between what the assay reports and the true value in that sample.
sese (standard error of concentration) The curve’s own estimate of the measurement SD for one sample.
Signal variance τ2\tau^2 True person-to-person (sample-to-sample) variance in the quantity of interest.
Total variance σ2\sigma^2 τ2+vi\tau^2 + v_i.
Weight ww 1/σ21/\sigma^2; precisely measured samples count more, but never more than 1/τ21/\tau^2.
Reliability λ\lambda τ2/σ2\tau^2/\sigma^2; fraction of the variance that is signal. Like an ICC.
Attenuation / regression dilution A noisy predictor makes the fitted slope too flat by about λ\lambda.
Censoring We know only that the value is below/above a limit.
Left / right / interval Below the lower limit / above the upper limit / between two limits.
Identifiability Whether the data contain enough information to tell two quantities apart.
REML Restricted maximum likelihood; the standard estimator for variance components.
Delta method A first-order approximation that converts the curve’s uncertainty into an SE for the concentration.
